articles.author: Microsoft
articles.body: [What and why]As Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication retire in Microsoft Entra ID, these methods will also become unavailable for SSPR. Organizations have 50 days after the applicable sign-in retirement rollout reaches their tenant to prepare alternative recovery methods. Users may still be able to sign in but lose the ability to reset forgotten passwords. Passkeys and other sign-in methods don't automatically satisfy SSPR requirements. Admins should identify affected users and ensure they have enough eligible recovery methods to prevent disruptions and increased helpdesk requests.[Rollout schedule]General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We expect rollout to begin and complete in February 2027User populationSign-in retirement rollout beginsSSPR transition endsUsers other than Global Administrators and external usersFebruary 1, 202750 days after this rollout reaches your tenantGlobal Administrators and external usersJuly 1, 202750 days after this separate rollout reaches your tenantThese are phased rollout start dates, not a single SSPR cutoff for every organization. Each population's 50-day period begins when its applicable rollout reaches your tenant. [Impact on your organization]Who is affectedOrganizations with users who rely on Microsoft-provided SMS/voice to meet their password-reset verification requirements. This includes users who have another sign-in method but still depend on SMS/voice for password recovery.Platforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra ID SSPRWhat will happenWhen the applicable sign-in retirement rollout reaches your tenant:50-day transition: Existing SMS and voice registrations remain usable for SSPR under your current recovery policy.Registration changes: SMS/voice SSPR registration and refresh prompts stop, but prompts for other eligible methods continue.My Sign-Ins: Users can no longer add SMS/voice methods or edit authentication phone numbers. Existing phone registrations appear disabled, even while usable for SSPR during the transition.Customer-managed telephony (CYOT): Recovery through supported providers remains available.After the 50-day transition period:Microsoft-provided SMS and voice are no longer available as SSPR recovery options.User's remaining eligible recovery methodsPassword-reset experienceEnough methods to meet the applicable SSPR requirementUser can continue resetting their password with those methodsNot enough methods to meet the applicable SSPR requirementUser cannot complete SSPR and is directed to contact their administratorThe applicable one/two method requirement still applies. To retain SMS/voice for recovery, your organization must configure a supported CYOT.Microsoft will not automatically change your SSPR policy or enable Allow password change after secure sign-in for your tenant.[Action required and recommendations]Prepare affected users before their applicable 50-day transition period ends:Identify affected users. Find users relying on SMS/voice for SSPR, even if they have other sign-in methods registered. Use the SMS and voice retirement and migration guidance.Prepare alternative recovery methods. Ensure users have enough eligible methods to meet SSPR policy requirements without Microsoft-provided SMS/voice. Passkeys alone don't satisfy SSPR requirements. If phone recovery is needed, configure and test a supported telephony provider before the transition ends.Test and communicate. Verify password recovery works with your SSPR policies and Conditional Access settings. Inform users and helpdesk staff about deadlines, registration steps, and support options.Recommended: Let passkey users change a forgotten passwordWhere available, administrators can enable Allow password change after secure sign-in for eligible users. Users can then sign in with their passkey and change their password in My Sign-Ins without knowing/entering their current password.Learn moreSMS and voice retirement and migration guidanceHow Microsoft Entra self-service password reset worksChoose a telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication[Compliance considerations]If your organization needs phone-based recovery for regulatory or operational reasons, plan and validate a supported customer-managed provider before the applicable SSPR cutoff.

articles.summary: Published: 2026-11-02Description Description Severity Notes On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed...
articles.author: Google Cloud
articles.body: Published: 2026-11-02Description Description Severity Notes On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked. Google Cloud infrastructure has not been breached. Security telemetry shows no evidence of exploitation against Google Cloud workloads. Applications built with the Google Cloud SDK Libraries are affected if their TLS trust store still accepts emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3, or AAA Certificate Services. The Google Cloud SDK Libraries themselves don't bundle CA certificates, with one exception: Java's com.google.api-client:google-api-client before 2.9.2. In all other cases, the trust store comes from a transport dependency (including the Google-maintained gRPC packages), the language runtime, or the operating system, so the fix is an update to those rather than to the Google Cloud SDK Libraries. In Java, Ruby, and PHP, upgrading the Google client libraries also pulls the fix in. The sections below give the action for each language. What should I do? Find your language below and apply the recommended actions. Then rebuild and redeploy your container images. Python The following packages are affected: certifi earlier than 2026.10.19 (REST transports). httplib2 earlier than 0.32.1, used by google-api-python-client and google-auth-httplib2; its bundled trust store is used when certifi is not installed. grpcio earlier than 1.84.1 (gRPC transports); bundled root store, does not read the operating system trust store. You can take the following actions to resolve these issues: Upgrade certifi to 2026.10.19 or later. Upgrade httplib2 to 0.32.1 or later. Upgrade grpcio to 1.84.1 or later. Patch releases for earlier release lines are being published; see GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh for the current list of fixed versions. Advisories: GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 (certifi), GHSA-2xm2-c8xx-p9vh (grpcio). Java The following packages and trust stores are affected: com.google.api-client:google-api-client earlier than 2.9.2, when the HTTP transport is created with GoogleNetHttpTransport.newTrustedTransport(). Versions earlier than 2.9.0 always use a bundled trust store that includes AAA Certificate Services; versions 2.9.0 and 2.9.1 use it when the Java Development Kit...

On Saturday, October 17, 2026, Google received a report from a security researcher regarding the compromise of private keys associated with eight eMudhra subordinate Certification Authority (CA) certificates, including those cross-signed by AAA Certificate Services. Consequently, these CA certificates are no longer trusted and are being revoked. Although Google Cloud infrastructure remains uncompromised, the following Google Cloud and Firebase products, base images, and client SDKs are impacted: Google Cloud CLI Cloud Shell Container-Optimized OS Compute Engine Google Kubernetes Engine Vertex AI Colab Enterprise App Engine Cloud Run Cloud Run functions Cloud Functions for Firebase Firebase App Hosting Cloud SQL AlloyDB for PostgreSQL Firestore Firebase App Distribution Cloud Monitoring Confidential Space Google Distributed Cloud Managed Service for Apache Spark Cloud Profiler Google Cloud SDK Libraries What should I do? Security telemetry shows no evidence of exploitation against Google Cloud workloads, and proactive mitigations are in place across Google-managed environments to block and distrust the affected certificate authority certificates. articles.author: Google Cloud
articles.body: Published: 2026-08-25Description Description Severity Notes A critical unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability exists in Next.js and libheif when processing malicious image files. Google Cloud infrastructure is not directly vulnerable, but customer workloads running Next.js on Google Cloud (e.g., Cloud Run, GKE, App Engine) may be affected. What should I do? Google Cloud backend services are not directly impacted, and no action is required to secure the underlying Google Cloud infrastructure. However, customers hosting Next.js applications on Google Cloud must take immediate action to secure their own workloads. We recommend that you manually upgrade your Next.js deployments to one of the following versions (or later) in your package.json: 16.3.3 15.5.24 Customers utilizing libheif should monitor for upstream OS patches and rebuild their container base images accordingly. Redeploy your updated workloads to ensure running containers utilize the patched versions. What vulnerabilities are being addressed? The vulnerabilities, GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 and GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497, allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code within the context of the application by supplying a crafted image file during Next.js image optimization. This issue occurs due to how the underlying libheif library processes clean aperture boxes in HEIF/AVIF images. High GHSA-2xp9-vwfh-vxw4 GHSA-g89c-p67h-r497

From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data...

articles.author: yuvalpery
articles.body: Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 contain a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder, according to the recently published CVE-2026-111497. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt decoder memory, expose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially run arbitrary code. Any application that decompresses untrusted Brotli data may be affected. This includes Node.js and Python applications that bundle the vulnerable decoder, and services that accept request bodies with the Content-Encoding: br header. We strongly recommend upgrading Brotli to a patched version: 1.0.10, 1.1.1 or 1.2.1 (Brotli releases). If you use Node.js, upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 (Node.js security release). If you can't patch your applications right away, Azure WAF on Application Gateway, Application Gateway for Containers and Azure Front Door can help mitigate the inbound attack vector, which is Brotli-compressed request bodies sent to your application. Note: Azure WAF inspects only inbound requests to your application. It can't protect applications that fetch and decompress Brotli-encoded responses from external servers. Those applications must be patched. Built-in protection enabled by default If you use Azure WAF with DRS 2.2 on Application Gateway or Azure Front Door Premium, you're protected by default against crafted Brotli-compressed request bodies. Rule 920450 (Paranoia Level 1, enabled by default) checks requests against a list of restricted headers, and DRS 2.2 adds Content-Encoding to that list. The rule has a critical anomaly score, so a single match blocks the request when the WAF policy is in Prevention mode. Earlier rule set versions don't restrict the Content-Encoding header. If you're still on DRS 2.1, CRS 3.2 or earlier, we recommend upgrading to DRS 2.2 to get the latest protection. To learn how, see Upgrade CRS or DRS ruleset version. If your application uses Next.js image optimization, apply the BlockNextImageCVE2026111497 custom rule below, even if you're on DRS 2.2. Custom rules to mitigate CVE-2026-111497 The custom rules block two attack vectors: 1. CVE2026111497 blocks any request whose Content-Encoding header includes the br (Brotli) coding, which this attack uses. DRS 2.2 already covers this vector through rule 920450. articles.summary: Microsoft analyzes a malicious Claude Code–branded extension, its persistent SSH backdoor, and guidance to detect and remediate it. The post Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research
articles.body: In this article Attack chain overviewAttack chainHost reconnaissance collectionSSH authorization and tunnel identitiesProtocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwardingPlatform-specific startup persistenceMitigation and protection guidanceImmediate actionsRemediation actionsFollow-up Investigation and recoveryMicrosoft Defender XDR detectionsThreat intelligence reportsMicrosoft Defender XDR Threat analytics Advanced hunting queriesMITRE ATT&CK techniquesIndicators of compromise (IOCs)Learn More On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace. Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails. Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete. articles.body: Updated October 30, 2026: We have updated this post with additional information as the feature is now generally available. Thank you for your patience. [What and why]Choose Your Own Telephony Provider (CYOT) is now generally available in Microsoft Entra ID. With CYOT, your organization can deliver SMS and voice authentication through a supported telecom provider of its choice. You purchase the provider's offer in Microsoft Security Store and manage the commercial relationship directly with the provider. Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication begins retiring on February 1, 2027. To keep SMS and voice authentication available for users who need it, set up CYOT before that date. Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant authentication methods, such as passkeys, instead of SMS or voice. Use telephony-based authentication only for users who have a business, regulatory, or technical need for it.[What you need to do]If your organization plans to use CYOT: Identify users who need SMS or voice. Confirm which users have a requirement that phishing-resistant methods can't meet. Choose a provider. Compare the supported telecom providers on coverage, channels, pricing, support, and compliance. Check purchasing requirements. Confirm that you have a paid Azure subscription that is eligible for Security Store purchases, and that you have the Owner role, or Contributor plus Role Based Access Control Administrator. Estimate costs. Review provider pricing and Azure hosting costs. Set up and roll out. Follow Set up SMS and voice. Start in evaluation mode, then increase traffic to your provider in stages. Complete your transition before February 1, 2027. articles.title: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
articles.summary: Teams support impersonation led to remote access, malicious runtime execution, and Certificate Services abuse through authentication relay and Kerberos. The post From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Sagar Patil, Jesse Birch and Tal Tzhori
articles.body: In this article Activity overviewAttack chain overviewPortable runtime staging and execution variantsHost discovery and AD CS assessmentCase 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusionCase 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identityWhy the response outcomes differedActionable investigation methodsReferencesLearn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths. Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication). This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? articles.body: As local agents have moved from experimentation into everyday work, traditional security visibility is no longer enough. Unlike static software, local agents such as coding assistants, command-line agents, desktop applications, and agentic development environments can operate on endpoints with access to a user's data, credentials, tools, and services. They can also connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that extend their access to additional tools and data. This change requires security teams to look beyond. They need to understand which local agents are running and where, which users and devices these agents are associated with, and which MCP servers these agents are configured to use. To address this challenge, at Microsoft Build 2026, we introduced new Microsoft Defender capabilities to help security teams discover and protect more than 20 types of local AI agents. Today, discovery of AI agents and their configured MCP servers on Windows and macOS is generally available, with discovery coverage expanded to more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers. On eligible, onboarded devices, Defender discovers supported agents by observing their activity and brings the agent, device, account, and configured MCP context together to give security teams visibility for their local agent environment. Beyond discovery, runtime protection for local agents for Windows continues to be available in preview, helping protect discovered agents as they operate. Teams can deploy runtime protection at scale from either the Microsoft Defender portal or the Microsoft Intune portal, with Intune-based deployment available in preview. Both discovery and runtime protection for local agents will be available for Microsoft Defender for Endpoint P2 and higher customers. See the local agents and associated MCPs operating in your environment In the Defender portal, security teams can see the discovered agents under Assets. The inventory associates each agent with the device and user account where it runs and includes details such as agent name, version, vendor, related process, and discovery history. articles.author: tejaskashyap
articles.body: Linux supports cloud services, containers, developer environments, business-critical applications, and a growing share of AI infrastructure. That makes Linux both essential to modern enterprises and increasingly attractive to attackers. AI is compressing the time required to research targets, vary payloads, and adapt when an attempt fails. Customers need protection that can recognize modern attacker behavior at runtime, continuously test effectiveness against realistic attacks, and learn and evolve with the threat landscape. That’s why Microsoft Defender is focused on three priorities for Linux: stronger runtime protection for fileless and in-memory attacks, continuous validation that proves protection remains effective, and AI-powered defense that can help security teams simulate attacks, investigate threats, close protection gaps, and reduce exploitable paths before compromise. A new Linux threat model The threat landscape has evolved from AI-assisted attacks, where people use AI to accelerate individual tasks, to AI-operated attacks, where AI coordinates more of the attack chain, and now it is moving to autonomous AI attacks that can adapt and act with limited human direction. Modern Linux attacks rarely depend on one file; they combine exposed services, stolen credentials, legitimate administration tools, scripts, containers, and cloud-native attack paths. As AI helps attackers generate and modify payloads at scale, adapt when an attempt fails, and move through the attack chain faster, defenders can no longer assume that every payload, script, or binary will resemble something they have seen before. Microsoft Security Research recently observed compromises involving a LiteLLM gateway, a RAGFlow deployment, and a Kestra workflow environment. The intrusion paths differed, but the objectives converged around credential theft, persistence, downstream access, and compute monetization. The broader lesson is that AI gateways, retrieval platforms, and orchestration services are becoming high-value control points where data, credentials, model connectivity, and workload execution meet. These examples also highlight a broader shift: attackers increasingly abuse legitimate services, tools, and workflows rather than relying solely on overtly malicious binaries. Viewed one event at a time, Bash, Python, curl, SSH, and network connections can appear legitimate. The security challenge is to understand their sequence, process relationships, destinations, and runtime...

The scheduling question Picture four Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) worker nodes with the same hardware. One keeps receiving new batch Jobs even as its CPU usage climbs. The natural question is: why does Kubernetes send another pod to a node that already looks busy? The answer is that the scheduler does not work like a live CPU load balancer. Capacity, allocatable, requests, and usage Term What it means Capacity The CPU and memory a node has. articles.author: Aarti Borkar
articles.body: October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months. A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed. At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish. For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter. Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report For builders: Build securely in the agentic era Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you. Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off. Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. articles.body: Attacks rarely stay in one channel. A flood of spam email, a Teams chat from an unfamiliar organization, and a call from "the helpdesk" can all be part of the same attempt. Security teams need a unified way to see where attacks are happening across email and collaboration, investigate them quickly, and show whether their defenses and users are improving. That's the job of our Detections and Insights reports. They're ready-to-use templates that turn Defender's email and collaboration data into views your team can use every day, as a Microsoft Sentinel workbook or a Power BI report. Today we're releasing version 4, which builds on Part 3 of this series, with new hunting queries and a new report for attack simulation training. Shaped by customer feedback, it helps you: See the attacks that matter with new Teams and impersonation views. Investigate faster with 125 new or improved hunting queries. Measure and improve resilience with a new attack simulation training report. articles.body: Updated October 26, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience. [What and why]Users will soon be able to register a passkey as their first multifactor authentication method. Previously, people had to set up an alternate MFA method like SMS or Voice before they could add a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO. That extra step pushed users toward weaker methods and slowed the move to phishing-resistant sign-in. Now password-only users can go straight to a passkey, making it easier to adopt strong authentication from day one. As part of this work, we will also be enabling Authenticator App passwordless sign-in to be a user's first registered MFA method. [Rollout schedule]This feature will roll out in phases: Phase 1: Support for synced passkeys, Microsoft Entra passkeys on Windows, and FIDO2 security keys. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early November 2026 (previously late October) and expect to complete by early January 2027 (previously late November 2026). Phase 2: Support for Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, Authenticator App passkey, and Authenticator App passwordless sign-in. General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We will begin rolling out in early January 2026 and expect to complete by late February 2027. [Impact on your organization]Who is affectedUsers who have not yet registered a multifactor authentication methodIdentity and security administrators responsible for authentication onboarding and registration policiesPlatforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra IDPasskeys (FIDO2)Windows Hello for BusinessmacOS Platform SSOMicrosoft Authenticator passwordless sign-inWhat will happenPassword-only users will be able to register passkeys or passwordless sign-in as their first MFA method.Users will no longer need to register a method such as SMS or voice before registering a passkey (FIDO2), Windows Hello for Business, macOS Platform SSO, or Authenticator passwordless sign-in.Organizations may see reduced registration friction and increased adoption of phishing-resistant authentication methods.Users who are enabled for passkeys will be prompted to register a passkey by default when completing applicable registration experiences, including those triggered by multifactor authentication (MFA) enforcement and Conditional Access authentication strengths. Security Defaults MFA registration prompts will adopt this experience in January–February 2027.[Action required and recommendations]No action is required for this change.We recommend that administrators:Review Conditional Access policies related to security information registration.Consider requiring MFA to register security information if additional verification is required by your organization.Review your user onboarding and registration guidance and update it as needed to reflect that eligible users may be prompted to register a passkey by default.Learn more (To be updated closer to rollout) Register a synced passkey (FIDO2) | Authentication | Microsoft Entra ID | Microsoft Learn[Compliance considerations]QuestionAnswerDoes the change include an admin control?Yes. Administrators can control which authentication methods users are allowed to register through existing Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access policies.Does the change affect access or authentication controls?Yes. The update changes how users register multifactor authentication methods by allowing eligible users to register supported passkeys or passwordless authentication methods as their first MFA method.Can administrators govern the feature through existing Microsoft Entra controls?Yes. Administrators retain control over the feature through Microsoft Entra authentication method policies and Conditional Access configurations.

articles.body: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website. Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. About the vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. articles.author: Oz_Wilder
articles.body: Email remains the most exploited gateway for cyberattacks, as the threat landscape continues to get more sophisticated with attackers using AI to scale phishing, malware, and business email compromise. Microsoft Defender is a leading email security solution, helping organizations stay ahead of these threats with a modern, cloud-native approach. At the same time, many organizations choose to layer additional email security solutions to meet compliance requirements or align to an existing defense-in-depth strategy. This approach can strengthen resilience, but it can also add operational complexity for SOC teams. That’s why one year ago, we introduced the Microsoft Defender Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem, which is designed to simplify that complexity by integrating partner protections into Microsoft Defender. Today, we’re continuing to expand the ICES vendor ecosystem by adding Proofpoint Core Email Protection API. Proofpoint joins existing members Darktrace, KnowBe4, Cisco, and VIPRE Security Group. How joint customers benefit from a streamlined SOC experience in Microsoft Defender The ICES ecosystem brings trusted third-party email security verdicts and telemetry into the Defender portal through an API-based integration model. This allows Microsoft Defender to acknowledge partner verdicts on messages, apply the highest-severity determination, and surface that information in the same investigation and response workflows security teams already use. The integration with Proofpoint Core Email Protection API is designed specifically for customers who have already chosen to deploy Proofpoint’s ICES solution alongside Microsoft Defender. It supports environments where customers run both solutions and want to reduce friction for their SOC teams. By integrating Proofpoint into the ICES ecosystem, customers can now preserve their existing security strategy while improving how investigations and response are carried out day to day. By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. articles.body: Amy Coleman, Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer, shared the below communication with Microsoft employees today. Today, we’re introducing a new Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) to eligible employees within participating organizations. This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs. The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we’re evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter. This builds on what we learned earlier this year through the Voluntary Retirement Program. What employees should know This offer will be available to eligible employees in participating teams in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below. This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs. Eligible employees will receive an email with a link to their Voluntary Exit Offer details within the next few hours. Looking ahead The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We’ll learn from it. At the same time, we’ll keep helping people focus on the work that matters most, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find new opportunities across Microsoft. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee. These are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute. My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving. Thank you for everything you continue to do for our customers, Microsoft and for one another. articles.author: JerryDevore
articles.body: Hi all. Jerry Devore dropping in for a minute to share some insights about the BlockNtlmv1SSO setting that went into effect with the October 2026 update. Why the change was necessary When MS-CHAPv2 is used for solutions like VPN, Wi-Fi, NPS, and RADIUS, the authentication flow leverages the MD4 hash of the account’s password to respond to a challenge. If that sounds familiar, then you have at least a basic understanding of NTLM. The problem is that this relic from 1998 (NT 4.0 SP4) produces a response to the challenge that is cryptographically equivalent to NTLMv1. So, while a device using MS-CHAPv2 can have NTLMv1 disabled, it is still exposing the same type of challenge response that makes NTLMv1 trivial to crack. The Change B ack in August 2025, an update added support for the registry setting BlockNtlmv1SSO (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0). The update did not create the registry setting, but it caused devices to start auditing for the use of "NTLMv1-derived credentials". With the October 2026 update, the default for Windows devices is to block the use of NTLMv1-derived credentials. This means that organizations that are still dependent on CHAPv2 are going to be impacted. Bracing for Impact For organizations that have already blocked NTLMv1 in their domains, there is no required action because MS-CHAPv2 using domain credentials is already impossible. For everyone else, you might want to do your due diligence before letting the October update rip if you are not certain whether you have any dependencies on MS-CHAPv2. The documentation for this change mentions events 4024 (Warning) and 4025 (Error) which are logged to the NTLM log of the client (Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational). Those events are extremely helpful, but very few organizations are forwarding the client NTLM logs to their SIEM. Possibly a better approach The October 2026 update giveth and the October update taketh away. What do I mean by that? Besides taking away NTLMv1-derived credentials, the update backported the enhanced NTLM auditing events to Server 2019 and Server 2022. As a result, you can leverage your domain controllers’ logs to determine if you have any MS-CHAPv2 dependencies prior to updating your endpoints. articles.author: Microsoft Security Research, Mahesh Mandava, Srinivasan Govindarajan, Sagar Patil and Suriyaraj Natarajan
articles.body: In this article Attack overview Technical detailsMitigation and protection guidanceIndicators of compromiseReferencesLearn More On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough. Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy. Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present. This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity. Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release. articles.author: CISA
articles.body: CISA, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (Cyber Centre), and partners are releasing joint guidance, Managing AI Token Consumption for Operational Resilience, to help organizations understand and manage token usage in support of operations. As organizations adopt third-party super intelligence (SI) services, token-based usage models can affect cost, performance, and access to critical services. Unmanaged token consumption may contribute to rising and unpredictable costs, reduced service availability, degraded performance, token exhaustion, and denial-of-tokens or denial-of-wallet attacks. The guidance outlines practical steps organizations can take to prioritize token allocation, design efficient workflows, improve user prompting practices, leverage caching and reusable context, optimize data before submission, and monitor token consumption over time. Critical infrastructure owners and operators can use this guidance to identify mission-critical functions that depend on SI, understand service provider and operational dependencies, and plan for reduced SI availability during outages, incidents, or periods of high demand. Cyber defenders can also use the guidance to manage SI-enabled cyber defense workflows while maintaining human oversight, governance, and strong cybersecurity fundamentals.

articles.author: Microsoft Security Research and Microsoft Threat Intelligence
articles.body: In this article What’s happeningWhat is ARTEX?Mitigation and protection guidanceReferencesLearn more As early as September 2026, Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours. Microsoft assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multi-tenant application. This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially. Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises. Storm-0940’s use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to Microsoft 365 customer environments through applications that had already been granted access. This allowed the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access. The activity conducted by the threat actor through the usage of ARTEX framework did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services. Although Microsoft identified Storm-0940-initiated authentication and follow-on activity in multiple customer environments, the presence of an affected application or successful threat actor authentication does not necessarily indicate that customer data was accessed or exfiltrated. It’s designed to help you quickly answer questions like: Which connectors are configured and which need attention? Which tables are receiving data? You’ll find it under Setup & configuration > Data & connectors, organized into three tabs: Overview, Connectors, and Tables. Overview: See health at a glance The Overview tab gives you a workspace-level snapshot of ingestion and health, so you can catch data issues before they impact analytics, detections, investigations, or reporting. It surfaces: Ingestion volume: Daily ingestion split by Analytics tier and Data Lake tier for your selected time range. Connectors that need attention: Connectors with credential errors, ingestion failures, or outages, including error type, failure count, and last successful ingestion. Table ingestion fluctuations: Tables with unexpected volume changes, grouped into spikes and drops. Data ingestion volume by table: Your top ingesting tables, ranked by daily volume. Ingestion latency by table: How long it takes for data to become available after it’s generated. Together, these insights help you troubleshoot connector failures, track down cost spikes, validate that new connectors are flowing, and catch unexpected changes in volume. Why we’re improving our billing model We heard two things consistently: cloud security pricing can be complex, and tracking cost can take real work. DWU simplifies this with one unit price. How DWU helps: Simplify pricing. Bring multiple workload-specific measures under one common billing model. Simplify onboarding and expansion. Make it easier to enable and extend protection across cloud environments. Match how you evaluate cloud security. Understand protection across your entire cloud environment, rather than workload by workload. Reduce cost-tracking friction. Make costs easier to estimate, track, and explain. One thing we deliberately kept unchanged: billing stays tied to what is used. How it compares DWU translates workload-specific usage into a common billing unit with a consistent per-unit price. Each workload continues to convert into DWUs according to its applicable usage measure. Workloads still count behind the scenes, including servers, databases, storage, containers, posture management, APIs, AI services, app services, Key Vault, and Azure Resource Manager. What changes are what customers see: one unit and one price. Workload-specific usage is converted into DWUs and aggregated across your environment, based on a consistent global per-unit price calculated hourly and billed monthly. Estimation, reporting, and billing use the same DWU framework, making it easier to understand how usage translates into cost. articles.body: Across my conversations with leaders in government, critical infrastructure and regulated industries, one priority consistently rises to the top: putting technology to work on their most important systems while maintaining the control those systems require. This challenge is becoming more important as advanced cloud and AI capabilities move into public services, regulated processes and essential operations. Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change. Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate. Last year, we introduced Microsoft Sovereign Cloud to give customers more choice in how they address these requirements. Since then, we have continued to turn our commitments into practical capabilities across public cloud and customer-operated environments, while expanding how we enable partners to address sovereignty requirements in their local markets. Today, we are sharing the next stage of that work. YouTube Video Click here to load media A continuum of control, built around the workload Our approach to digital sovereignty starts with the workload. Each workload carries different requirements for data, operations, technology dependencies, continuity and risk. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed to make it easier for organizations to apply the appropriate level of control to each workload without forcing every application into the same deployment model. Those needs can vary widely across organizations. A public-facing digital service may benefit from the scale and pace of innovation in the public cloud. A system supporting essential operations may need to continue running locally if connectivity is disrupted. An AI workload handling highly sensitive data may require models, data and processing to remain within a customer-controlled environment. Microsoft Sovereign Cloud is designed around this workload-based approach, providing a continuum of management, control and options across Sovereign Public Cloud, Sovereign Private Cloud and the Sovereign Partner Ecosystem. articles.author: Hayete Gallot
articles.body: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted. This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise. Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic...

articles.author: Nadim Abdo
articles.body: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Learn how to secure your agentic estate at speed and scale Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”Satya Nadella Project Perception—Securing your agentic insider We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. articles.author: aws@amazon.com
articles.body: Bulletin ID: 2026-139-AWS Scope: AWS Content Type: Important (requires attention) Publication Date: 10/16/2026 10:15 AM PDT Description: FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP is an open-source, thread-safe TCP/IP stack for the FreeRTOS kernel, distributed by Amazon for use on embedded and IoT devices. AWS identified two issues with FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP, affecting multiple versions. CVE-2026-102551: improper verification of the source of a communication channel in the IPv6 Router Advertisement handler. The handler does not fully validate that a received Router Advertisement originates from an on-link source before acting on it. Under certain conditions, a remote third-party might influence an endpoint's IPv6 gateway, prefix, and address configuration, potentially enabling interception of the device's IPv6 traffic. This issue is reachable in the library's default configuration, where ipconfigUSE_IPv6 and ipconfigUSE_RA are both enabled. CVE-2026-102552: improper verification of the source of a communication channel in the DNS resolver. The resolver does not fully validate that a DNS reply originates from the server that was queried before accepting it. Under certain conditions, a remote third-party might insert a chosen address into the device's DNS cache, potentially redirecting the device's subsequent connections for the affected name. Impacted versions: - CVE-2026-102551 (Router Advertisement): <= V4.4.1 - CVE-2026-102552 (DNS resolver): <= V4.4.1 Please refer to the article below for the most up-to-date and complete information related to this AWS Security Bulletin.

articles.title: Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
articles.summary: New whitepaper from Microsoft and NVIDIA helps enterprises manage open-weight AI model risks with a shared taxonomy, evaluations, and controls. The post Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
articles.author: Michael Scovetta
articles.body: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework. The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards. Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise Understanding risk in the deployment context Open- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools. The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access,...

articles.body: In this article Uncovering the shadow world of a phishing kit ecosystemStorm-3119: YAM Store, the power brokerStorm-2990: The Iron Man System phishing kitDownstream activity from Storm-2990 phishing kitsMitigation and protection guidanceMicrosoft Defender detectionsHunting queries Over the past year, Microsoft uncovered a Chinese-language cybercriminal ecosystem, an interconnected network of phishing kit operators, developers, and an illicit marketplace selling tools and infrastructure for large-scale phishing, enabling cybercriminal operations worldwide. articles.author: ChristianFriedel-Jain
articles.body: By: Christian Friedel-Jain - Sr. Security Consultant | James Noyce - Sr. Security Solution Engineer Introduction Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) are among the most sensitive endpoints in any organization. A PAW, in most of our Microsoft consulting projects, exists to do one job safely: administer cloud services from a hardened device that is only ever allowed to reach a small, tightly controlled set of internet destinations. But an endpoint’s security posture is ultimately defined by its behavior under failure conditions. When we moved the internet access restriction for our PAW devices from a locally enforced restriction (more about that later) to a solution based on Microsoft Global Secure Access (GSA), we immediately identified a gap under failure conditions – but first a quick grounding on the moving parts. Global Secure Access (What is Global Secure Access?) is Microsoft’s umbrella term for Microsoft Entra Internet Access and Microsoft Entra Private Access — the components of Microsoft’s Security Service Edge solution. For a PAW device we are leveraging Microsoft Entra Internet Access as an identity centric secure web gateway solution to control exactly which internet destinations the workstation can reach, by applying a fine-grained set of rules and policies enforced through Conditional Access in Microsoft Entra. This configuration provides us better filtering capabilities, like web content filtering (Global Secure Access web content filtering) with TLS inspection (TLSi) (Global Secure Access transport layer security inspection) and additional features like Threat Intelligence (Global Secure Access threat intelligence), but it comes also with a downside. Currently by default, if the GSA client encounters an issue or cannot connect to its required GSA edge services, the GSA client will fall back to a fail-open state, rather than to a fail-close state. Difference between those two modes: Fail-Open: When a security or control mechanism fails, access is still allowed. Fail-Close: When the security or control mechanism fails, access is blocked. This blog post covers above problem and showcases a solution we built, as part of our projects, to achieve a “Fail-Close” state rather than having the current “Fail-Open” behavior. articles.body: Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. articles.author: Vytas_Boyev
articles.body: Potentially Unwanted Applications, or PUA, they aren't necessarily malware, but they are applications you probably don't want running across your environment either. Microsoft defines potentially unwanted applications as software that can adversely affect endpoint performance or use. Examples include advertising software, software bundlers, and applications that use behaviors intended to evade security products. Microsoft Defender can also consider an application's reputation when determining whether software qualifies as potentially unwanted. That sounds straightforward. On Windows, it generally is. On Linux, finding the resulting audit events requires knowing exactly where to look. And that is where things get interesting. PUA, PUP… Same Neighborhood, Slightly Different Address Before going further, it is worth clearing up some terminology. Across the security industry, you will commonly encounter both PUP, or Potentially Unwanted Program, and PUA, or Potentially Unwanted Application. The terms are frequently used for software that isn't necessarily malicious but has characteristics that make its presence undesirable, such as intrusive advertising, bundling additional software, or other behavior the user might not have knowingly requested. Microsoft uses Potentially Unwanted Application (PUA) as its product and detection terminology. Microsoft specifically distinguishes PUA from malware. A PUA might cause poor system performance, display unexpected advertisements, install other software, or have a poor reputation because of undesirable behavior, but those characteristics don't automatically make the application malware. Microsoft's classification criteria include examples such as: Advertising software that displays advertisements or promotions, including injecting advertisements into webpages. Bundling software that offers to install additional software that isn't digitally signed by the same entity, or that itself qualifies as PUA. Evasion software that actively attempts to avoid detection by security products or behaves differently when security software is present. Applications that have developed a poor reputation based on undesirable behavior. Microsoft's broader software-classification model also distinguishes between unknown software, malware, unwanted software, and other classifications. Software can therefore be legitimate and functional while still meeting Microsoft's criteria for classification as potentially unwanted. For the rest of this...

articles.body: Updated October 8, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience.[What and why]Microsoft Entra ID will support passkey registration and sign-in for B2B users, including internal guest users and external users. Eligible B2B users will be able to register and use passkeys issued by the resource tenant to satisfy that tenant's multifactor authentication (MFA) requirements.Passkeys are already supported for member users in their home tenant. Until now, B2B users could not use a resource tenant passkey when that tenant required MFA and did not trust the home tenant's MFA. This update closes that gap and gives guest and external users a phishing-resistant way to satisfy MFA requirements in the resource tenant.B2B users can register a resource tenant passkey from the resource tenant's My Security Info page, during a proof-up prompt, or through a passkey registration campaign. Once registered, the passkey can satisfy the resource tenant's MFA requirements during sign-in.Microsoft Authenticator app passkeys will be supported for internal guest users but not for external users.Important: This rollout intersects with the previously announced retirement of SMS and voice authentication. As described in Message Center posts MC1426371 and MC1434201, any user enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policies will be automatically enabled for all passkey types. This will include eligible B2B users when B2B passkey support becomes available.[Rollout schedule]General Availability (GCC, Worldwide): Beginning in late October 2026, with a phased rollout as outlined below:Internal guest users: Beginning in late October 2026 (previously early October) and is expected to complete by late November 2026 (previously late October)External users (excluding Microsoft Authenticator app passkeys): Rollout timing will be communicated in a future Message center post update.[Impact on your organization]Who is affectedMicrosoft Entra administrators managing Authentication methods policiesOrganizations that use Microsoft Entra B2B collaborationInternal guest users and external users who are in scope for passkey authenticationInternal guest users and external users who are enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policiesPlatforms and servicesMicrosoft Entra IDMy Security InfoAuthentication methods policyConditional AccessWhat will happenThe feature will be enabled by default.B2B users who are already in scope for passkeys in your Authentication methods policy will automatically be able to register and sign in with resource tenant passkeys.Eligible B2B users may receive prompts to register a passkey during sign-in through proof-up experiences or passkey registration campaigns, if those experiences are configured in your tenant.Users can also register a passkey from the resource tenant's My Security Info page.If your organization has excluded B2B users from passkeys in the Authentication methods policy, and those users are not separately subject to automatic passkey enablement through the SMS and voice retirement changes, they will not be prompted and will not be able to register or sign in with a resource tenant passkey.Under the SMS and voice retirement changes described in MC1426371 and MC1434201, B2B users who are enabled for SMS or voice in the Authentication methods policy or legacy MFA policies will be automatically enabled for all passkey types. Excluding these users from the passkey policy alone will not prevent this automatic enablement if they remain enabled for SMS or voice.This change gives guest and external users a phishing-resistant sign-in option and helps organizations extend strong authentication requirements to their B2B population.[Action required and recommendations]No action is required.We recommend that administrators review current passkey and MFA configurations before rollout:Review your Authentication methods policy. Confirm which users are in scope for passkeys, including guest and external users. B2B users who are in scope will be enabled automatically. Exclude them from the policy if that is not the intended behavior.Review Message Center posts MC1426371 and MC1434201 for details about the SMS and voice retirement changes.Review SMS and voice assignments in both the Authentication methods policy and legacy MFA policies. If you do not want specific B2B users to be automatically enabled for all passkey types, move those users off SMS and voice in all applicable policies. Excluding them only from the passkey policy is not sufficient while they remain enabled for SMS or voice.Review your passkey registration campaign. Confirm that the campaign's user scope includes the intended users.Review your Conditional Access policies. Confirm that MFA and authentication strength requirements will apply as intended for B2B users when resource tenant passkeys become available.Confirm user scoping across authentication-related policies. Make sure the groups and user types targeted by each policy align with your organization's requirements for guest and external users.Consider notifying your help desk and identity support teams that eligible B2B users may begin receiving passkey registration prompts after rollout.[Compliance considerations]QuestionAnswerDoes the change store new customer data?Passkey credential registration data may be stored as part of Microsoft Entra authentication management.Does the change alter how existing customer data is processed, stored, or accessed?The change introduces an additional authentication method for B2B users accessing resource tenant resources.

articles.author: JamesAde
articles.body: Email remains one of the most common entry points for security threats. Yet email products often describe the same activity with different table names, fields, and values. This makes it harder to build detections and investigations that work consistently across data sources. The Microsoft Sentinel Advanced Security Information Model, or ASIM, EmailEvent schema is now available. It provides a common structure for email delivery and inspection events, helping customers and partners create security content that works across supported email data sources. A consistent view of email security activity EmailEvent standardizes the information analysts need to understand what happened to an email and why. It covers: Email delivery and inspection events Sender, source, and recipient information Message subject, size, direction, and delivery location URLs and file attachments SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication results Delivery actions such as delivered, blocked, quarantined, or deleted Threat, risk, confidence, tactic, technique, and remediation details Instead of learning a different data model for every product, analysts can query the normalized EmailEvent fields. Parser developers map each source's native data to the same schema. How it works Consider an email that contains a suspicious attachment. The email security product records the sender, recipients, attachment, authentication results, inspection verdict, and final action. A connector collects that event. A parser or Data Collection Rule maps the source fields to EmailEvent. Microsoft Sentinel can then query the normalized record using the same field names used for other supported email sources. This common structure separates security content from the details of a specific product. When another source adds an EmailEvent parser, existing source-independent queries and detections can work with that source without being rewritten around its native field names. Why it matters Simpler analytics: Write queries against one consistent set of email fields. Broader coverage: Apply source-independent security content across normalized email sources. Faster investigations: Compare delivery, authentication, attachment, URL, and threat details without translating different data models. Easier integration: Give connector and parser developers a defined contract for bringing new email telemetry into ASIM. EmailEvent does not replace the rich native data produced by email security products. It provides a consistent...
